title: Game Development & Low-Level Programming
tagline: How games and operating systems really work, from bits to engines
description: What a computer is really doing when a game runs: bits, memory and addresses, the CPU and assembly, Windows and its processes, debuggers, game engines, modding and the kernel. You read, experiment with live simulations, and build real projects in Visual Studio. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course.

milestones.title: How Computers Run Programs
milestones.blurb: The machine underneath everything else: what the CPU does with a program, how numbers are stored as bits, and how memory and addresses work.

lessons.title: What Happens When a Program Runs
lessons.summary: A computer does one small thing at a time. It **fetches** an instruction from memory, works out what it means, and **does it**. Everything a game does, from drawing a frame to saving your progress, is billions of those small steps.

lessons.title: Bits, Bytes and Hexadecimal
lessons.summary: Memory holds only **bits**, switches that are on or off. Eight bits make a **byte**, and **hexadecimal** is a shorthand that writes a byte as two digits. Once you can read hexadecimal, a screen full of memory stops looking like noise.

lessons.title: Memory, Addresses and Pointers
lessons.summary: Memory is one long row of numbered bytes. A variable is a few of those bytes with a name, its **address** is the number of its first byte, and a **pointer** is a variable whose value is an address.

lessons.title: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code
lessons.summary: The CPU only understands numbers, so C++ has to be translated before it can run. Four tools do it in turn: the **preprocessor**, the **compiler**, the **assembler** and the **linker**. Knowing what each one does explains most build errors and almost everything you will see in a debugger.

lessons.title: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look
lessons.summary: When a function is called, the CPU has to remember where to come back to, and the function needs somewhere to keep its local variables. Both go on the **stack**, a region of memory that grows by one **frame** per call and shrinks again when the call returns.

lessons.title: What the Operating System Does for a Program
lessons.summary: Between your program and the hardware sits the **operating system**. It loads the program into memory, gives it a private **address space**, shares the CPU between hundreds of programs, and is the only way to reach files, the screen or the network. Each of these ideas gets its own chapter later; this lesson is the map.

lessons.title: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course
lessons.summary: The examples on this site run in your browser, but from chapter 4 on you will build real Windows programs, step through them in a debugger and read their memory. That takes **Visual Studio** on your own PC. This lesson installs it with the right parts, creates a console project, and sets the options the course assumes.

lessons.title: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change
lessons.summary: A **debugger** pauses a running program so you can look inside it. This lesson walks through a first session in Visual Studio: setting a **breakpoint**, stepping one line at a time, reading variables in the **Locals** and **Watch** windows, and opening the **Memory** window to watch the bytes of a variable change.

milestones.title: Memory in Depth
milestones.blurb: Where every value in a running program lives, how long it lives there, and what goes wrong when code gets that wrong.

lessons.title: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses
lessons.summary: Lesson 1.05 introduced the stack. This lesson looks at a real x64 Windows frame: the **return address**, the 32-byte **shadow space**, saved registers, locals and the 16-byte alignment rule. It also covers how big the stack is, how recursion uses it, and how to replace deep recursion with a loop.

lessons.title: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time
lessons.summary: The stack is fast but small, and everything on it disappears when its function returns. For data whose size or lifetime is only known at run time (a level loaded from disk, a list of bullets), programs ask the **heap** for memory. This lesson shows how `new`, `delete`, smart pointers and containers use it, what it costs, and what a Debug build does to help you catch heap mistakes.

lessons.title: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory
lessons.summary: Besides the stack and the heap, a running program has memory that exists for its whole life: its **code**, its **constants** and its **global and static variables**. These come straight from the `.exe` file, in named **sections**. Knowing the layout tells you at a glance what kind of thing an address points to.

lessons.title: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
lessons.summary: An object's **lifetime** runs from the end of its construction to the start of its destruction. Outside that window its memory may still be there, but using it is a bug. This lesson traces lifetimes for locals, temporaries, heap objects and members, and introduces **RAII**: tying every resource to an object's lifetime so it is released automatically.

tasks.title: Undo it on the way out

lessons.title: Alignment and Padding in Detail
lessons.summary: Every type has an **alignment**: the addresses it may start at must be a multiple of it. To keep each member of a struct aligned, the compiler inserts unused **padding** bytes. This lesson gives the exact rules, shows how to predict a struct's size and members' offsets, and how to arrange members so less memory is wasted.

lessons.title: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
lessons.summary: A class in memory is only its data members, laid out by the alignment rules. Member functions, `static` members and access specifiers take no space in the object. Inheritance puts the base class's members first, and a class with virtual functions gains a hidden pointer at the front. Knowing this lets you read any object's bytes in a debugger.

lessons.title: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
lessons.summary: An array is the simplest data structure there is: elements side by side, with no gaps and no bookkeeping. Element `i` is at the start address plus `i` times the element size. Two-dimensional data such as a tile map is stored the same way, one row after another. This lesson shows the arithmetic, why the order you loop in matters for speed, and how games store grids.

lessons.title: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
lessons.summary: Text in memory is a run of numbers, one or more per character. A **C string** is a `char` array ending in a zero byte. `std::string` keeps its own length and stores short text inside the object itself. And which numbers stand for which characters depends on the **encoding**: ASCII, UTF-8, or the UTF-16 that Windows uses internally.

lessons.title: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
lessons.summary: Memory bugs are the hardest bugs in C++ because the symptom often appears far from the cause, or only sometimes. This lesson names the main kinds (**buffer overruns**, **use after free**, **double free**, **uninitialised reads** and **leaks**), shows what each one looks like when it strikes, and gives the habits that prevent them.

lessons.title: Catching Memory Bugs with AddressSanitizer
lessons.summary: **AddressSanitizer** (ASan) is a compiler feature that adds a check to every memory access. It stops the program at the exact moment of a buffer overrun or use after free, and prints where the memory was allocated, where it was freed and where it was misused. Visual Studio supports it with one switch. This lesson shows how it works and how to read its reports.

lessons.title: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio
lessons.summary: The Memory window shows raw bytes, and this chapter has given you everything you need to read them. This lesson puts it together: setting the window's display, recognising pointers, Debug patterns, text and floating-point numbers at a glance, and decoding a whole object by hand.

tasks.title: Read values out of raw bytes

milestones.title: Pointers, References and Data Structures
milestones.blurb: Pointers used the way real programs use them: chains of objects, function pointers, virtual calls, and the containers that hold a game's world.

lessons.title: Pointers to Pointers
lessons.summary: A pointer is a variable, so it has an address too, and a pointer can hold that address. A **pointer to a pointer** lets a function change which object another pointer points at, and it is how arrays of pointers, command-line arguments and many Windows API "out" parameters work.

lessons.title: Following Pointers Through Objects
lessons.summary: Real programs are webs of objects joined by pointers: a world holds a player, a player holds an inventory, an inventory holds items. Getting from one object to another means following a **chain** of pointers, each step a read of an address and an offset. This lesson shows what that looks like in memory, how to follow it safely, and what it costs.

lessons.title: References Under the Hood
lessons.summary: A reference looks like a second name for an object, and in the language that is exactly what it is. In the machine, a reference that has to be stored or passed is an address, the same as a pointer. This lesson shows both views, the rules that make references safer than pointers, and the ways they can still dangle.

lessons.title: Function Pointers and Callbacks
lessons.summary: Functions live in memory too, so they have addresses, and a variable can hold one. A **function pointer** lets code decide at run time which function to call: the basis of callbacks, command tables, state machines and plugin systems. This lesson covers raw function pointers, `std::function` and lambdas, and what each costs.

lessons.title: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
lessons.summary: A `virtual` call picks the function to run from the object's real type, at run time. Compilers do it with a **vtable**: a table of function pointers, one per class, and a hidden **vptr** in every object pointing at its class's table. This lesson shows the layout, walks through a virtual call step by step, and explains what it costs.

lessons.title: Linked Lists from Scratch
lessons.summary: A **linked list** stores each element in its own node, and each node points to the next. Inserting and removing anywhere is cheap, but finding anything means following pointers one at a time. Building one by hand is the best practice there is for pointers, and it explains why games use them rarely and carefully.

lessons.title: How std::vector Really Works
lessons.summary: `std::vector` is three pointers and a heap block. Its **size** is how many elements are in use, its **capacity** how many fit before it must grow. When it grows, it allocates a bigger block, moves everything across and frees the old one, which is why pointers into a vector can suddenly dangle. Knowing this lets you use the most important container in C++ efficiently.

lessons.title: Hash Tables
lessons.summary: A **hash table** finds a value by its key in about the same time however many entries it holds. A **hash function** turns the key into a number that picks a **bucket**, and the table only has to look in that one place. This lesson explains hashing, collisions and load factor, compares `std::unordered_map` with `std::map`, and shows where games use them.

tasks.title: A hash table with open addressing

lessons.title: Trees and Graphs
lessons.summary: When data has branches rather than a single line, pointers or indices join it into **trees** and **graphs**. Games are full of them: the scene graph of objects attached to other objects, the binary search tree inside `std::map`, the graph of rooms in a dungeon, and the grid a monster searches to find the player. This lesson covers the shapes, the two ways to walk them, and a shortest-path search.

lessons.title: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
lessons.summary: A game creates and destroys objects constantly: bullets, particles, enemies, pickups. This lesson puts the chapter together into the structures engines use for them: dense arrays with swap-and-pop, **object pools** with free lists, and **generational handles** that let code refer to an object safely even after it has been destroyed and its slot reused.

milestones.title: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
milestones.blurb: Solutions, projects and configurations, what the compiler and linker each do, libraries and DLLs, and a proper introduction to the debugger.

lessons.title: Solutions, Projects and Build Configurations
lessons.summary: A real game is not one `.cpp` file. It is a **solution** holding several **projects**, such as the game, an engine library, a tools DLL and a test runner, each built in several **configurations** and for one or more **platforms**. This lesson shows how Visual Studio organises that, where the settings live, and how to set up a multi-project solution you will reuse for the rest of the course.

lessons.title: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
lessons.summary: Lesson 1.04 introduced the four build stages. This lesson goes deeper into the rules that decide which file needs what: **declarations** versus **definitions**, headers and include guards, the **one definition rule**, `inline` and `static`, and how the linker matches **symbols** between object files. These rules explain almost every "already defined" and "unresolved" error you will meet.

lessons.title: Reading Compiler and Linker Errors
lessons.summary: Build errors look intimidating because one mistake can produce a screen of messages. This lesson gives a method (find the first error, read its code, go to its line, ignore the cascade), and a field guide to the MSVC errors and warnings you will meet most often, with what each usually means.

lessons.title: Static Libraries
lessons.summary: A **static library** (`.lib`) is a bundle of object files. Linking it into a program copies in the parts the program uses, so the result is one self-contained `.exe`. This lesson builds the course's `engine` library, shows how the linker pulls code out of it, and covers the settings that must match between a library and the program that uses it.

lessons.title: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL
lessons.summary: A **DLL** is a library that stays a separate file and is joined to a program when it runs. This lesson builds a DLL, exports functions from it, uses it in the two ways Windows offers (**load-time linking** through an import library, and **run-time loading** with `LoadLibrary` and `GetProcAddress`), and covers the rules about `DllMain`, memory and C++ types across the boundary.

lessons.title: Managing Dependencies with vcpkg
lessons.summary: Real projects use other people's libraries: a window and input library, an image loader, a user interface toolkit. **vcpkg** is Microsoft's package manager for C and C++: you list the libraries a project needs in a `vcpkg.json` file, and it downloads, builds and links them with settings that match your project. This lesson sets it up for the course's later chapters.

lessons.title: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack
lessons.summary: Lesson 1.08 was a first session. This lesson covers the debugger as a daily tool: every way of controlling execution (run to cursor, step into a specific call, set the next statement), moving around the Call Stack, breaking when an exception is thrown, Just My Code, and attaching to a program that is already running.

lessons.title: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows
lessons.summary: The debugger's windows show a paused program's state at every level, from C++ expressions down to CPU registers and machine instructions. This lesson covers the tricks that make them far more useful: **format specifiers**, **pseudo-variables**, viewing arrays through pointers, the **Registers** and **Disassembly** windows, and how they connect to everything in chapters 1 to 3.

lessons.title: Conditional and Data Breakpoints
lessons.summary: A plain breakpoint stops every time. In a game loop that runs 60 times a second, that is useless. **Conditions**, **hit counts** and **filters** make a breakpoint stop only when it matters; **tracepoints** log without stopping; and **data breakpoints** stop on the exact instruction that changes a piece of memory, which is the fastest way to find who corrupted a value.

lessons.title: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes
lessons.summary: A Release build runs the same source code many times faster, because the optimiser rewrites it: it keeps values in registers, inlines functions, removes work whose result is unused, and assumes your code has no undefined behaviour. This lesson shows each transformation, explains why some bugs only appear in Release, and sets up a build that is both optimised and debuggable.

projects.title: What kind of build is this?

milestones.title: The Windows API
milestones.blurb: Talking to the operating system directly: handles, errors, files, windows and messages, and loading code at run time.

lessons.title: Handles and Kernel Objects
lessons.summary: Files, threads, processes, events and many other resources are **kernel objects**: they live inside the Windows kernel, and your program refers to them only through **handles**. This lesson explains what a handle is, the rules for getting and closing one, the two different "invalid" values, and how to wrap handles in an RAII class so they can never leak.

tasks.title: An owner for any kind of handle

lessons.title: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
lessons.summary: The Windows API reports failure in several ways: a `BOOL` that is `FALSE`, a null or invalid handle, an `HRESULT`, or a status code. The details usually come from `GetLastError`. This lesson shows each pattern, how to turn an error number into a readable message, how `HRESULT`s are built, and how to read a Microsoft documentation page so you know which pattern a function uses.

lessons.title: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
lessons.summary: Most Windows API functions that take text exist twice: an **A** version for 8-bit "ANSI" strings and a **W** version for UTF-16 "wide" strings. Windows works in UTF-16 internally; the rest of the world, and most libraries, use UTF-8. This lesson explains the A/W split, why the course always calls the W functions, and how to convert between UTF-8 and UTF-16 at the edges of your program.

lessons.title: Files and Directories
lessons.summary: Games read assets and configuration and write save files and logs. This lesson uses the Windows file API directly (`CreateFileW`, `ReadFile`, `WriteFile`), shows where a game should keep its files, how to list a directory, how to save without ever leaving a half-written file, and when the portable `std::filesystem` and `std::fstream` are the better choice.

lessons.title: Windows and the Message Loop
lessons.summary: A Windows program with a window does not ask "has a key been pressed?". Windows tells it, by putting **messages** in a queue that the program reads in a **message loop** and hands to a **window procedure**. This lesson explains window classes, messages, the loop, and the variant games use so they can keep rendering when no messages arrive.

lessons.title: A First Win32 Application
lessons.summary: Put the last lesson together into a complete windowed program: `wWinMain`, registering a class, creating a window, a game-style loop, and drawing a moving square with GDI using a back buffer so it does not flicker. About 120 lines of plain Windows API, and every one explained.

lessons.title: Keyboard, Mouse and Timers
lessons.summary: Input arrives as messages whose details are packed into `wParam` and `lParam`. This lesson unpacks them: virtual-key codes, the bits of a key message, typed characters, mouse coordinates and buttons, and when to read the keyboard's current state instead. It ends with timers and the high-resolution clock that games use for timing.

lessons.title: Loading Libraries at Run Time
lessons.summary: Lesson 4.05 loaded a DLL of your own. This lesson looks at the loader's side: the **search order** Windows uses to find a DLL, why that order is a security risk and how to restrict it, finding modules that are already loaded, getting a module's file path, using functions that only exist on newer versions of Windows, and **delay loading**.

lessons.title: The Console API
lessons.summary: The console window is more than a place for `std::cout`. With the console API and **virtual terminal sequences** you can move the cursor, use colours, hide the cursor, read individual key presses and redraw a whole screen without flicker: enough for a text-mode game or a live tool display. This lesson covers both the classic API and the modern escape sequences.

tasks.title: Build a frame for the console

milestones.title: Processes, Threads and Virtual Memory
milestones.blurb: What a process is, how every process gets its own address space, how threads share it, and how Windows decides who may touch what.

lessons.title: Programs, Processes and Modules
lessons.summary: A **program** is a file; a **process** is a running instance of one, with its own address space, threads and handles; a **module** is an executable or DLL loaded into a process. This lesson makes the distinction concrete by starting a child process, waiting for it, reading its exit code, and passing it a command line.

lessons.title: Virtual Address Spaces
lessons.summary: Every address a program uses is **virtual**: the processor translates it, page by page, into a physical location in RAM using **page tables** the operating system maintains for each process. This lesson explains the translation, the size and shape of a 64-bit address space, why some addresses are impossible, and what happens when a page is not in RAM at all.

lessons.title: Pages, Protection and Committing Memory
lessons.summary: Under the heap sits `VirtualAlloc`, which manages memory directly in pages. A region of the address space can be **free**, **reserved** (set aside, but with no memory behind it) or **committed** (backed by memory), and every committed page has a **protection**: readable, writable, executable, or none. This lesson uses these tools directly, and shows how games use them for huge growable arrays, guard pages and catching bugs.

lessons.title: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery
lessons.summary: `VirtualQuery` answers "what is at this address?": the region's start and size, its state, protection and type. Walking it across the whole address space produces a map of your process: the modules, heaps, stacks and reserved areas. This lesson builds that map, the same view tools like VMMap show, and uses it to identify what any pointer points at.

lessons.title: Threads and the Scheduler
lessons.summary: A **thread** is a path of execution with its own registers and its own stack, running inside a process and sharing everything else. The **scheduler** decides which threads run on which cores and for how long. This lesson creates threads with `std::thread` and the Windows API, splits work between them, and explains what the scheduler does with them.

lessons.title: Data Races, Mutexes and Events
lessons.summary: When two threads use the same memory and at least one writes, without coordination, the result is a **data race**: undefined behaviour that shows up as lost updates, torn values and bugs that vanish under the debugger. This lesson shows a race, then the tools that prevent them: **mutexes**, **atomics**, **condition variables** and Windows **events**, and the classic trap of **deadlock**.

tasks.title: A job queue for worker threads

lessons.title: Listing Processes and Modules
lessons.summary: Task Manager, Process Explorer and every debugger start by asking Windows "what is running?". This lesson uses the **Tool Help** API to list running processes and the modules loaded in your own process, the building block of crash reporters, launchers that check whether the game is already open, and the tools in chapter 12.

lessons.title: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No
lessons.summary: "Access is denied" (error 5) is Windows checking rights. Every process carries a **token** saying who it runs as; every securable object has a **security descriptor** saying who may do what; and every handle is opened for specific **access rights**. This lesson explains the check, **integrity levels** and UAC, **protected processes**, and the principle of asking for no more than you need.

lessons.title: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses
lessons.summary: Run a program twice and its code, heap and stack land at different addresses. That is **ASLR**, a security feature. This lesson explains why it exists, how a module that can load anywhere still works (**relocations** and RIP-relative code), how to turn any address into a stable **module + offset (RVA)** form, and why raw pointers must never be saved in files.

tasks.title: Turn an address into module + offset

milestones.title: x64 Assembly Language
milestones.blurb: The language the CPU actually runs. You learn to read what the compiler produces and to write small routines yourself.

lessons.title: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
lessons.summary: x64 assembly is the text form of the machine code your C++ becomes. This chapter teaches you to read it, and occasionally to write it. It starts with the **registers**, the processor's handful of built-in variables, their 64, 32, 16 and 8-bit names, and the shape every instruction follows: an operation and its operands.

lessons.title: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
lessons.summary: Most instructions in real code just move data: between registers, from memory into a register, from a register back to memory. This lesson covers `mov` and its widening relatives `movzx` and `movsx`, the **addressing modes** that let one instruction compute an address like `base + index × scale + offset`, and `lea`, which does that arithmetic without touching memory at all.

lessons.title: Arithmetic and Bit Operations
lessons.summary: The arithmetic instructions (`add`, `sub`, `imul`, `inc`, `dec`, `neg`, `div`) and the bit instructions (`and`, `or`, `xor`, `not`, `shl`, `shr`, `sar`) are the processor's whole calculator. This lesson covers each, the **flags** they set as a side effect, and the tricks compilers use, such as replacing division by a constant with multiplication.

lessons.title: Flags, Comparisons and Jumps
lessons.summary: Every `if`, loop and `switch` in C++ becomes a **comparison** that sets the flags and a **conditional jump** that reads them. This lesson covers `cmp` and `test`, the family of `j`*cc* jumps and which ones mean signed or unsigned, and the branch-free alternatives `setcc` and `cmov`.

lessons.title: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret
lessons.summary: Four instructions manage the stack from lesson 1.05 at the machine level. `push` and `pop` add and remove 8-byte values; `call` pushes a return address and jumps; `ret` pops it and jumps back. This lesson steps through them, shows a function's **prologue** and **epilogue**, and explains what a corrupted stack does to `ret`.

lessons.title: The Microsoft x64 Calling Convention
lessons.summary: A **calling convention** is the agreement between a caller and the function it calls: where arguments go, where the result comes back, which registers survive the call and who cleans up the stack. On 64-bit Windows there is one convention for everything. Knowing it lets you read any function's arguments in the debugger, follow calls in disassembly, and write assembly that C++ can call.

lessons.title: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch
lessons.summary: Control flow in C++ compiles into a small set of recognisable shapes built from comparisons and jumps. This lesson teaches you to recognise them: `if` and `if`/`else`, `while` and `for` loops (and how compilers rotate them), short-circuit `&&` and `||`, and the **jump table** a `switch` becomes. Recognising shapes is how you read disassembly quickly.

lessons.title: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
lessons.summary: In assembly there are no types, only addresses and sizes. A struct member is a fixed offset from a pointer; an array element is base plus index times size; a pointer chain is a series of loads. This lesson shows how each C++ data access compiles, and how to work backwards from the offsets and sizes in disassembly to the data structures behind them.

tasks.title: Rebuild a struct from its accesses

lessons.title: Floating Point with SSE
lessons.summary: x64 code does floating-point maths in the 16 **xmm** registers with **SSE** instructions. Scalar instructions like `addss` work on one `float`; packed ones like `addps` work on four at once, the start of **SIMD**. This lesson reads typical game maths in assembly: loading constants, arithmetic, comparisons, conversions between ints and floats, and a first look at vectorised code.

lessons.title: Writing Assembly Functions with MASM
lessons.summary: Microsoft's assembler, **MASM** (`ml64.exe`), ships with Visual Studio. This lesson writes a few functions in assembly, adds them to a C++ project, and calls them from C++, following the calling convention by hand. Writing even a little assembly makes reading it much easier, and shows exactly what the compiler does for you.

lessons.title: What Optimised Code Looks Like
lessons.summary: Release builds rarely look like their source. Functions disappear into their callers, loops are unrolled and vectorised, variables never touch memory, and branches become arithmetic. This lesson is a field guide to the transformations you will meet in optimised disassembly, so that you can map it back to the C++ (or, when reverse engineering, to something like it).

projects.title: An encoder for a few instructions

milestones.title: Debugging and Diagnostics
milestones.blurb: Finding out why a program misbehaves: call stacks, crash dumps, symbols, logging, WinDbg and profilers.

lessons.title: Thinking Like a Debugger
lessons.summary: Debugging is a method, not a talent. This lesson sets out the method experienced engineers use: make the bug happen reliably, form a hypothesis, test it with the smallest possible experiment, and narrow the search by halving it. It covers **minimal reproductions**, **bisecting** code and history, and the habits that make the tools in the rest of this chapter effective.

lessons.title: Call Stacks and Symbols
lessons.summary: A call stack turns a crash address into a story: which function, called from where, with what. Making that work needs **symbols**: the `.pdb` files that map machine code back to names and source lines. This lesson covers what is in a PDB, how debuggers find the right one, Microsoft's **symbol server** for Windows' own DLLs, how stacks are walked without frame pointers, and how to capture a stack trace from inside your own program.

lessons.title: Asserts and Logging That Help
lessons.summary: The best bugs to fix are the ones the program reports itself, at the moment things go wrong. **Asserts** check assumptions and stop immediately when one is false; **logs** record what happened so you can reconstruct it later. This lesson shows how to write both well: `static_assert` and `assert`, a better assert macro, log levels, and a ring buffer that keeps the last moments before a crash.

lessons.title: Crash Dumps
lessons.summary: When a game crashes on a player's machine, you cannot attach a debugger. A **crash dump** captures the crashed process's state (threads, stacks, registers, some or all memory) into a file you can open later in Visual Studio or WinDbg as if you had been there. This lesson explains exception codes, writing a **minidump** from your own crash handler, collecting dumps with Windows Error Reporting, and opening them.

lessons.title: A First Look at WinDbg
lessons.summary: **WinDbg** is Microsoft's command-line-driven debugger. It does everything Visual Studio's debugger does and much more, opens any crash dump, and is the only debugger for the Windows kernel (chapter 16). This lesson installs it and teaches the two dozen commands that cover nearly all everyday work, mapped to the Visual Studio windows you already know.

lessons.title: Debugging Optimised Code
lessons.summary: Some bugs only appear in Release builds, and crash dumps from players are always from optimised code. Debugging it is harder (variables vanish, lines run out of order, functions disappear into their callers) but entirely possible. This lesson gives a practical toolkit: make Release builds debuggable, read values from registers and the disassembly, switch optimisation off selectively, and use logging where stepping fails.

lessons.title: Debugging Threads
lessons.summary: Multithreaded bugs are timing-dependent, so they hide when you look for them. This lesson covers the tools that make them visible: naming threads, the **Threads** and **Parallel Stacks** windows, freezing threads to force an ordering, diagnosing **deadlocks** from call stacks, and finding races with careful logging and data breakpoints.

lessons.title: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
lessons.summary: When a game is slow, the cause is almost never where you would guess. A **profiler** measures where the time actually goes. This lesson covers the two kinds of profiler (**sampling** and **instrumenting**), Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool, frame-based instrumentation with scoped timers, and how to read the results to find the few places worth optimising.

milestones.title: Reverse Engineering Fundamentals
milestones.blurb: Understanding a program from its compiled form, practised on programs you build yourself: file formats, static and dynamic analysis, and rebuilding data structures.

lessons.title: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules
lessons.summary: **Reverse engineering** means working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. It is how security researchers find vulnerabilities, how malware is analysed, how old software is kept running and how file formats are documented for interoperability. This lesson sets out what it involves, the tools, and the legal and ethical ground rules this course follows.

lessons.title: The PE File Format
lessons.summary: Every `.exe` and `.dll` on Windows is a **Portable Executable** (PE) file: a set of headers describing the program, followed by its **sections** of code and data. This lesson walks through the headers in order (the DOS header and `MZ`, the `PE` signature, the file header, the optional header and its data directories, and the section table) and reads them from C++.

lessons.title: Imports, Exports and the Loader
lessons.summary: A program's **import table** lists every function it uses from DLLs; a DLL's **export table** lists every function it offers. Together they are a map of what a program can do and how its modules connect. This lesson reads both, explains the **import address table** that the loader fills in at start-up, and shows how to convert RVAs to file offsets so tables can be read from a file on disk.

lessons.title: Static Analysis with a Disassembler
lessons.summary: A **disassembler** turns a program's machine code back into assembly and organises it into functions, cross-references and control-flow graphs; a **decompiler** goes one step further, to C-like pseudocode. This lesson sets up **Ghidra**, the free, open-source reverse engineering suite, and walks through analysing a small program you built yourself: finding `main`, reading the listing and the decompiler side by side, and annotating as you learn.

lessons.title: Recognising Functions, Loops and Branches
lessons.summary: Disassemblers find most functions automatically, but understanding a function means recognising its parts: where it starts and ends, what its arguments and result are, and how its control flow maps to `if`, loops and `switch`. This lesson turns chapter 7's patterns into a reading routine for unknown functions, and covers the cases where automatic analysis gets function boundaries wrong.

lessons.title: Recognising Classes, Vtables and Strings
lessons.summary: C++ programs leave distinctive traces even without symbols: **vtables** in read-only data list each polymorphic class's virtual functions, **RTTI** records often hold class names outright, constructors write vptrs, and **strings** reveal messages, file names and formats. This lesson shows how to find and use each, and how a `strings`-style scan works.

lessons.title: Dynamic Analysis with a Debugger
lessons.summary: Static analysis shows every path a program could take; **dynamic analysis** shows what it actually does, with real values. This lesson uses a debugger on a program without its source (**x64dbg** as well as the debuggers you know): breaking on API calls, watching arguments and return values, following indirect calls, and tracing the path through code to confirm what static analysis suggested.

lessons.title: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
lessons.summary: A **cross-reference** (xref) records that one place in a program refers to another: a call to a function, a read of a global, a use of a string. Following xrefs, backwards to "who uses this?" and forwards to "what does this use?", is how you navigate an unknown program. This lesson covers the kinds of xref, how disassemblers find them, and how to decode a `call` instruction's target yourself.

lessons.title: Reconstructing Structs from Compiled Code
lessons.summary: Types disappear in compilation, but every struct leaves a trail of offsets and sizes in the code that uses it. This lesson is a step-by-step method for rebuilding a struct definition from those accesses, combining static evidence (offsets, sizes, instructions used) with dynamic evidence (values seen in the debugger), and recording the result as a type the disassembler can apply everywhere.

lessons.title: Practice Targets You Compile Yourself
lessons.summary: The best way to learn reverse engineering is on programs whose source you can check afterwards. This lesson gives a graded series of practice targets to write, build without symbols, and analyse with the chapter's tools, from a single function to a small game with classes and a file format, along with how to set up the builds and how to check your answers.

milestones.title: Game Engine Architecture
milestones.blurb: How a game is put together: the loop, time, entities, rendering, input, resources and saving.

lessons.title: The Game Loop
lessons.summary: Every real-time game is built around one loop that runs as long as the game does: read **input**, **update** the world, **render** a frame, repeat, dozens of times a second. This lesson builds that loop step by step, explains what belongs in each phase, and shows how an engine is organised around it.

lessons.title: Time Steps and Frame Rates
lessons.summary: How much time does each update simulate? Using the real frame time (a **variable time step**) is simple but makes physics behave differently on fast and slow machines. Most games run the simulation at a **fixed time step**, consuming real time from an **accumulator**, and smooth the picture with **interpolation**. This lesson builds that loop and covers frame limiting and vsync.

lessons.title: Entities, Components and Systems
lessons.summary: How should a game represent its thousands of objects? Deep inheritance trees (`Monster : Character : Entity`) become rigid and slow. Many engines use **entity-component-system** (ECS) design instead: an **entity** is just an id, **components** are plain data attached to it, and **systems** are loops over every entity with a given set of components. This lesson explains why, and builds a small ECS on the **sparse set** structure.

lessons.title: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
lessons.summary: Rendering turns the game's state into pixels, mostly on the **GPU**. This lesson follows a frame from the CPU's side (what to draw, culling, sorting, **draw calls**) through the GPU's pipeline (**vertex shaders**, **rasterisation**, **pixel shaders**, depth testing) to the screen, with the coordinate transforms in between. It is a map for the graphics work in chapter 11 and beyond.

lessons.title: Input Handling
lessons.summary: Raw input (keys, mouse buttons, gamepad sticks) is not what game code should depend on. Engines turn it into **actions** ("jump", "move left"), track for each one whether it was **pressed**, **held** or **released** this frame, and let players **rebind** the keys. This lesson builds that layer, and covers gamepads, dead zones and input buffering.

lessons.title: Loading and Managing Resources
lessons.summary: Textures, sounds, models, levels and fonts are **resources**: large, loaded from disk, shared between many users, and expensive to load twice. A **resource manager** loads each one once, hands out **handles** to it, counts who is still using it, unloads it when nobody is, and ideally loads in the background. This lesson designs one, and covers asset pipelines and hot reloading.

lessons.title: Game State and Save Files
lessons.summary: Saving a game means deciding what state matters, writing it in a format that will still load after the game is updated, and never leaving a corrupted file behind. This lesson covers what to save and what to rebuild, binary and text formats, **versioning** and migrating old saves, **checksums** that detect damage, and writing files safely.

lessons.title: Scripting and Data-Driven Design
lessons.summary: Engines get faster to work with when behaviour and content move out of C++ and into **data**: monster stats in a file, levels from an editor, dialogue in a table, and, for logic, **scripts** in an embedded language such as Lua. Designers can then change the game without recompiling it. This lesson covers data files, a small configuration parser, embedding a scripting language, and the trade-offs.

lessons.title: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game
lessons.summary: One of the best ways to learn engine architecture is to read a real one. Many shipped games and engines have released their source. This lesson is a method for approaching a large, unfamiliar codebase: building it, finding the main loop, tracing one feature end to end, and recognising the patterns from this chapter in someone else's code.

milestones.title: Building a Small Game
milestones.blurb: A complete little dungeon game in C++, built step by step. It becomes the practice target for the tools and mods in later chapters.

lessons.title: Project Setup and a Window
lessons.summary: This chapter builds a complete small game, a top-down dungeon crawler called **Delve**, using the ideas from chapters 1 to 10. It starts here: a Visual Studio project with **SDL2** from vcpkg, a window and renderer, and the fixed-time-step game loop from lesson 10.02. By the end of the chapter you will have a game with a map, a player, monsters, items, levels, saves and a debug console.

lessons.title: Drawing a Tile Map
lessons.summary: Delve's world is a grid of tiles stored in a flat array (lesson 2.07) and loaded from a plain text file (lesson 10.08), where each character is a tile and special characters mark where the player and monsters start. This lesson writes the level format, the loader with validation, and the renderer that draws the visible part of the map around a camera.

lessons.title: A Player That Moves
lessons.summary: Delve is turn-based on a grid: each key press moves the player one tile, and the world (monsters, doors) responds. This lesson connects lesson 10.05's input actions to movement, handles walls, doors and stairs, adds key repeat for held keys, and makes moves look smooth by sliding between tiles in the renderer only.

lessons.title: Monsters and Simple AI
lessons.summary: Delve's monsters need to notice the player, chase them around walls, and attack when adjacent. This lesson gives each monster a small **state machine**, and replaces per-monster pathfinding with one **distance map** (a breadth-first search from the player, lesson 3.09) that every monster follows downhill. It is simple, fast, and the basis of AI in many roguelikes.

lessons.title: Health, Items and Inventory
lessons.summary: Combat and loot turn Delve into a game. This lesson adds health and attack components, a damage formula with a little randomness, death and drops, item definitions loaded from data, pickups, and an inventory where identical items **stack**. Every number lives in a data file, so balancing never needs a rebuild.

lessons.title: Levels and Saving
lessons.summary: Delve gets several floors connected by stairs, and the ability to save and continue. This lesson handles level transitions (what persists between floors and what is rebuilt), designs Delve's save format using lesson 10.07's header, version and checksum, and writes it safely, so a crash or power cut never costs the player their run.

lessons.title: A Debug Console
lessons.summary: Every serious game has a hidden console for its developers: press a key, type `god`, `give potion 5` or `goto 3`, and test anything without playing up to it. This lesson builds Delve's console from lesson 3.04's command table: text input, a command registry with help text, argument parsing, history, output, and a rule that keeps it out of the shipped game.

lessons.title: Polish and Packaging
lessons.summary: The difference between a working prototype and a game people enjoy is **polish**: feedback for every action, a little motion, sound, and no rough edges. The difference between a game on your machine and one on a friend's is **packaging**: a Release build with everything it needs, version information, and a test on a clean system. This lesson finishes Delve.

milestones.title: Inspection and Debugging Tools
milestones.blurb: Standalone tools that watch a running program from outside, built for the course's own game: a memory viewer, a value finder and a live stats panel.

lessons.title: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs
lessons.summary: Development tools often need to see inside a running game from a separate program: a stats panel, a level editor that previews live, a profiler. Each process has its own private memory (lesson 6.02), so tools need a deliberate channel. This lesson surveys the documented ways (the game publishing data through **shared memory**, **pipes** or sockets; the **debugging API** for a process you start; dumps) and builds a shared-memory channel, the method the rest of this chapter uses.

lessons.title: A Memory Viewer
lessons.summary: A hex viewer that shows raw memory with addresses, bytes and text is one of the most useful debugging tools there is, and the Memory window of lesson 2.11 is one. This lesson builds one for your own process and for a process your tool launched: reading with **ReadProcessMemory**, coping with pages that cannot be read, and formatting the classic three-column view.

lessons.title: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
lessons.summary: Visual Studio, WinDbg and x64dbg are all built on the same Windows **debugging API**. This lesson uses it directly to write a tiny debugger: it launches a program of yours as its debuggee, receives **debug events** (process and thread creation, DLL loads, exceptions, debug output, exit), reports them, and continues. It demystifies every debugger you have used, and is the core of crash-catching tools.

lessons.title: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
lessons.summary: Delve will publish its live state (frame time, floor, the player's health and position, monster count) in shared memory for tools to read. The hard part is consistency: the game writes while the tool reads, so the tool must never see half an update. This lesson designs the shared block with a header and version, and protects it with a **sequence lock**, a lock-free scheme where the writer never waits.

lessons.title: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
lessons.summary: With Delve publishing its telemetry, a separate tool can show it live: frame times with a graph, the floor, the player's health and position, how many monsters are alive. This lesson builds that tool as a console program (chapter 14 gives it a graphical interface): finding running copies of the game, reading snapshots on a timer, keeping a history for graphs, and coping when the game starts, stops or restarts.

lessons.title: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
lessons.summary: The game will change: new fields in the telemetry, new commands on the pipe. Tools built for last month's game should keep working, and new tools should cope with old games. This lesson designs for that: **append-only** layouts with a size field, version and capability checks, feature flags, and the rules that let both sides evolve without breaking each other.

tasks.title: Can this tool read that game?

lessons.title: Testing and Hardening a Tool
lessons.summary: A tool that crashes, hangs or shows wrong numbers is worse than none: people stop trusting it. This lesson hardens the chapter's tools: treating everything read from another process as untrusted input, validating snapshots, timeouts and reconnection, running with least privilege, and testing the logic separately from the platform code, including deliberately feeding it garbage.

milestones.title: Modding and Runtime Instrumentation
milestones.blurb: How games are extended: data mods, scripting, plugin systems and instrumentation, practised on your own game and on games that support modding.

lessons.title: How Games Support Mods
lessons.summary: Many of the most loved games owe much of their life to **mods**: changes and additions made by players. Games that support modding on purpose provide layers for it: replaceable data and assets, scripting, plugin APIs and official editors. This lesson surveys those layers, how mods are found and loaded in order, how conflicts arise, and the responsibilities that come with letting other people's code run inside your game.

lessons.title: Data Mods and Scripting
lessons.summary: The simplest and safest mods change data. This lesson gives Delve a **layered file system** that looks for each file in the enabled mods (last first) before the base game, then improves on whole-file replacement by **merging** data entries so several mods can change different things in the same file. It ends by opening the game's scripting to mods, with limits.

lessons.title: Designing a Plugin Interface
lessons.summary: A plugin is native code built separately from the game, possibly with a different compiler version, that the game loads at run time. The interface between them must therefore be a stable **C interface**: plain types, function pointers, explicit versions and sizes. This lesson designs Delve's plugin API in both directions (the **host API** the game offers plugins, and the **plugin API** plugins offer the game) using lessons 4.05, 3.04 and 12.06.

lessons.title: Plugins as DLLs
lessons.summary: With the interface designed, Delve can load plugins: find each enabled mod's DLL, load it safely, call its entry point, validate what it returns, order plugins by their dependencies, call them each frame, and unload them cleanly. This lesson writes the plugin manager, and adds **hot reloading** of your own plugins during development.

lessons.title: Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
lessons.summary: **Instrumentation** means adding observation points to a program: measuring how long functions take, counting calls, recording events, letting plugins react to what happens. The cleanest way is to design the points in from the start: scoped timers, an **event bus** that plugins and tools subscribe to, and indirection through function pointers where behaviour should be replaceable. This lesson builds those, and looks at compiler-assisted instrumentation for your own builds.

lessons.title: A Debug Menu Inside the Game
lessons.summary: A console is fast for people who remember commands; a **debug menu** drawn over the game is faster for everyone else: checkboxes for god mode and map reveal, sliders for monster speed, buttons to spawn things, live graphs. This lesson registers **tweakable** variables in one place, draws them with Dear ImGui (previewing chapter 14), and lets plugins add their own sections.

lessons.title: Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
lessons.summary: A game with mods is a platform other people build on. This lesson covers the architecture that keeps it stable: isolating failures so one broken mod cannot take the game down, budgets for mod work, keeping saves safe, versioning everything mods touch, diagnosing problems from players' reports, and the honest limits of isolating native code.

lessons.title: Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools
lessons.summary: Many games ship official modding support: editors, mod kits, scripting APIs and workshop integration. Working with them is the most productive and least fragile way to mod other people's games. This lesson covers what official tools usually provide, how to learn an unfamiliar one, the licensing of mod content, and how the design ideas of this chapter look from the modder's side.

milestones.title: User Interfaces for Tools
milestones.blurb: Giving your tools a face: immediate-mode interfaces with Dear ImGui, layouts, tables, plots and settings.

lessons.title: Immediate-Mode Interfaces
lessons.summary: Most application toolkits are **retained mode**: you create widget objects once and keep them in sync with your data. **Immediate mode** turns that around: every frame, code describes the whole interface with function calls, and each call both draws its widget and reports what the user did. This lesson explains the model, why it suits tools and games so well, and how it works underneath, with **ids**, **hot** and **active** widgets.

lessons.title: Setting Up Dear ImGui
lessons.summary: Dear ImGui is a small, widely used C++ library for immediate-mode interfaces. It does not draw anything itself: **back ends** connect it to a platform (for windows and input) and a renderer (for drawing). This lesson sets it up with vcpkg and the SDL2 back ends used by Delve, explains the per-frame calls, fonts and DPI scaling, and builds a standalone tool application for chapter 12's tools.

lessons.title: Windows, Widgets and Layout
lessons.summary: This lesson covers the ImGui toolkit you will use in every tool: windows and child regions, the common widgets (text, buttons, checkboxes, sliders, inputs, combos), how ImGui lays widgets out (top to bottom by default, `SameLine` to go across, groups, columns of fixed width), ids in loops, and disabling widgets.

lessons.title: Tables, Trees and Plots
lessons.summary: Tools mostly show data: lists of entities, hierarchies of objects, numbers over time. ImGui's **tables** give sortable, resizable, scrollable columns; **trees** show hierarchies such as a scene graph; **plots** show values over time. This lesson uses each for Delve's tools, including clipping long lists so a table of ten thousand rows stays fast.

lessons.title: Settings That Persist
lessons.summary: A tool that forgets its window positions, open panels and last connection every time it starts is tiring to use. ImGui saves window layout itself to an `.ini` file; your tool saves its own settings alongside. This lesson covers both, where to store them, versioning them, and the classic bug of windows restored onto a monitor that is no longer connected.

tasks.title: Keep a restored window on screen

lessons.title: A Complete Tool Window
lessons.summary: This lesson assembles the chapter into one application: **Delve Inspector**, a tool with a docked layout that connects to a running copy of Delve and shows its live stats, monsters, a memory view of the telemetry block and a command panel, with a command palette, settings that persist, and the hardening from chapter 12. It is the template for the tools in chapter 18's capstones.

tasks.title: Fuzzy matching for a command palette

milestones.title: Windows Kernel Architecture
milestones.blurb: The other half of the operating system: user mode and kernel mode, system calls, the memory and I/O managers, and why kernel code needs such care.

lessons.title: User Mode and Kernel Mode
lessons.summary: Lesson 1.06 introduced the kernel as the part of Windows with full control of the hardware. This chapter looks inside. It starts with the boundary itself: the processor's **privilege levels**, what runs in **kernel mode** (the kernel, the HAL, drivers), how kernel memory is shared by all processes, and why code running there must be held to a far higher standard than anything in user mode.

lessons.title: System Calls: Crossing the Boundary
lessons.summary: Every time a program opens a file, allocates memory or waits on an event, it crosses from user mode into the kernel and back. This lesson follows one call, `CreateFileW`, through **kernelbase.dll** and **ntdll.dll** to the `syscall` instruction and into the kernel's system service dispatcher, and explains the rule that makes the boundary safe: the kernel never trusts anything that comes from user mode.

lessons.title: Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
lessons.summary: Lesson 5.01 showed handles from the user's side. Inside the kernel, the **object manager** creates every kernel object (files, processes, threads, events, devices, registry keys), gives each a header with its type, reference counts and security, keeps a **namespace** of named objects, and maintains each process's handle table. This lesson looks at all of that, and at the object names drivers use.

tasks.title: Resolve a path through symbolic links

lessons.title: The Memory Manager
lessons.summary: The kernel's **memory manager** provides every process's virtual address space (chapter 6) and also manages kernel memory. This lesson covers the kernel side: **paged** and **non-paged pool**, why the difference matters so much in drivers, **pool tags** for tracking allocations, **memory descriptor lists** (MDLs) for describing buffers, and how the memory manager handles page faults.

lessons.title: The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
lessons.summary: Every read, write and device request in Windows becomes an **I/O request packet** (IRP) handed to a **stack** of drivers by the **I/O manager**. This lesson explains IRPs, driver and device objects, how a request travels down a device stack and its completion travels back up, the kinds of drivers (filter, function, bus), and the frameworks (WDM and KMDF) drivers are written with.

tasks.title: Send a request down a device stack

lessons.title: Interrupts, IRQLs and Scheduling
lessons.summary: Hardware demands attention at any moment through **interrupts**, and the kernel must decide what can interrupt what. Windows does this with **interrupt request levels** (IRQLs). The IRQL a piece of code runs at decides what it may do: whether it can wait, touch paged memory, or be preempted. This lesson explains the levels, **DPCs**, **spin locks**, and the rules that cause the most famous blue screen of all.

lessons.title: Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
lessons.summary: When kernel-mode code fails, Windows stops the machine with a **bug check** (the blue screen) rather than risk corrupting data. This lesson explains why, what the stop code and parameters mean, the most common driver bug checks, how kernel crash dumps are collected and read with `!analyze`, and how **Driver Verifier** turns rare driver bugs into immediate, diagnosable ones.

lessons.title: Building a Virtual Machine Lab
lessons.summary: Kernel experiments belong in a **virtual machine**: a whole Windows installation running as a program on your PC, which can crash, be debugged from outside, and be restored to a clean state in seconds. This lesson sets up the lab used by chapter 16: a Windows VM with **snapshots**, **test signing** enabled inside it, kernel debugging from the host with WinDbg over the network, and the habits that keep your real machine safe.

milestones.title: Educational Driver Development
milestones.blurb: Writing, loading and debugging a small, harmless driver inside a virtual machine, to see the kernel from the inside.

lessons.title: Installing the Windows Driver Kit
lessons.summary: Drivers are built with the **Windows Driver Kit** (WDK), an extension to Visual Studio that adds kernel headers and libraries, driver project templates, signing, deployment and analysis tools. This lesson installs matching versions of Visual Studio, the SDK and the WDK on the host, creates the chapter's driver project, and explains what is different about building kernel code.

lessons.title: A Driver That Says Hello
lessons.summary: The smallest useful driver has two functions: **DriverEntry**, called when it loads, and an **unload** routine, called when it is removed. This lesson writes them, prints to the kernel debugger, loads the driver in the lab VM as a service, watches its messages in WinDbg, and unloads it, the complete cycle every later lesson builds on.

lessons.title: The Driver Lifecycle
lessons.summary: A driver sets things up in `DriverEntry` (devices, links, memory, timers) and must tear every one of them down in its unload routine, in reverse order, leaving nothing behind. If set-up fails halfway, it must undo exactly the steps that succeeded. This lesson builds that discipline: the load and unload sequence, the service registry key, cleanup on partial failure, and why anything left behind after unload crashes the machine.

lessons.title: Device Objects and Symbolic Links
lessons.summary: For a user program to talk to a driver, the driver needs a **device object** to receive requests and a **symbolic link** that gives it a name user mode can open. This lesson creates both in `DriverEntry`, removes them in unload, controls who may open the device with a **security descriptor**, and adds the create and close dispatch routines that make opening and closing work.

lessons.title: IOCTLs: Talking to a Driver
lessons.summary: Reads and writes move bytes; most driver interfaces need **commands**: "echo this", "give me your statistics", "reset". Those are **I/O control codes** (IOCTLs), sent with `DeviceIoControl` and received as `IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL`. This lesson explains how a control code packs device type, function, buffering method and required access into 32 bits, and writes the driver's dispatch routine for the echo driver's commands.

lessons.title: A User-Mode Client
lessons.summary: The other half of the driver is an ordinary program: it opens the device by its symbolic link with `CreateFileW`, sends commands with `DeviceIoControl`, and reports errors clearly. This lesson writes the echo driver's client using chapter 5's handles and errors, wraps the protocol in a small class, and covers the details that trip people up: buffer sizes, `ERROR_MORE_DATA`, and the driver not being loaded.

lessons.title: Validating Buffers and Staying Safe
lessons.summary: A driver that accepts requests from user mode is a doorway into the kernel, and many serious Windows vulnerabilities have been driver bugs in exactly this code. This lesson covers the three ways buffers reach a driver (**buffered**, **direct** and **neither** I/O), and the rules that keep a driver safe: check every length, never return more than was written, never leak kernel memory, and handle every failure.

lessons.title: Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
lessons.summary: With WinDbg attached to the lab VM (lesson 15.08), you can break into your driver's code, step through it, and inspect every kernel structure involved in a request. This lesson is a working session: breakpoints on driver load and on dispatch routines, debug output with levels, examining driver and device objects and IRPs with `!drvobj`, `!devobj` and `!irp`, and analysing a bug check your driver caused.

lessons.title: Test Signing
lessons.summary: 64-bit Windows loads only kernel drivers with a trusted digital signature: **driver signature enforcement**. During development, drivers are signed with a **test certificate** and loaded on machines in **test mode**, which is why the lab VM has it on. This lesson explains how signing works, sets up test signing, explains how real drivers are signed for release, and why test mode belongs only in a lab.

lessons.title: Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine
lessons.summary: This project assembles chapter 16 into a complete, working pair: the **XenonEcho** driver with ping, echo and statistics commands, and its client. It gives the full driver source with every rule from the chapter applied, a build-load-test-unload checklist for the lab VM with Driver Verifier on, a test plan including hostile inputs, and a note on what KMDF would do for you.

milestones.title: Testing, Security and Reliability
milestones.blurb: Making low-level code you can trust: tests, sanitizers, fuzzing, secure coding and the integrity of software you do not own.

lessons.title: Unit Tests for Low-Level Code
lessons.summary: Every practice task in this course has been checked by unit tests. This lesson turns that around: writing tests for your own low-level code with a framework such as Catch2 or GoogleTest, structuring code so it can be tested (pure logic, injected clocks, random numbers and platform calls), and deciding what is worth testing in games, tools and drivers.

lessons.title: Sanitizers and Static Analysis
lessons.summary: Tools find bugs that tests and reviews miss. **Sanitizers** add checks while the program runs (AddressSanitizer for memory, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer for undefined behaviour); **static analysis** examines the code without running it (compiler warnings, MSVC's `/analyze`, clang-tidy, annotations). This lesson sets up each for a Visual Studio project and shows the classes of bug each one catches.

lessons.title: Fuzzing
lessons.summary: **Fuzzing** feeds a program huge numbers of automatically generated, mostly broken inputs and watches for crashes, hangs and sanitizer reports. Coverage-guided fuzzers such as **libFuzzer** learn which inputs reach new code and mutate those further, finding bugs no human would think to test. This lesson writes fuzz targets for Delve's parsers, runs them with MSVC's fuzzer support and AddressSanitizer, and minimises the crashing inputs.

lessons.title: Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
lessons.summary: Security bugs are ordinary bugs in code that handles input an attacker can control. This lesson collects the course's lessons into secure coding practice for C++: **trust boundaries**, the classic bug classes (buffer overruns, integer errors, use after free, path traversal, format strings, time-of-check to time-of-use), and the habits and safe building blocks that prevent them.

lessons.title: Threat Modelling
lessons.summary: A **threat model** is a structured answer to "what could go wrong, and what are we doing about it?" written before the code, not after the breach. This lesson walks through the four questions of threat modelling, draws a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, applies **STRIDE** to find threats systematically, and ranks them so effort goes where it matters. The worked example is Delve with mods, saves and an online leaderboard.

lessons.title: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
lessons.summary: This course taught how programs look from the inside, which is also how cheats and tampering work. This lesson takes the defender's side: why a game can never fully trust the client, why **server authority** is the foundation of fair online play, how to verify the integrity of your own files and updates with hashes and code signing, what client-side anti-tamper can and cannot do, and the legal, ethical and privacy limits that apply to both sides.

lessons.title: Performance Without Guessing
lessons.summary: Programmers are famously bad at guessing where time goes. This lesson replaces guessing with measurement: frame budgets, **profilers** (Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool and sampling in general), microbenchmarks done properly, and the statistics that make timings trustworthy (medians and percentiles instead of averages). It ends with the common real causes of slow C++: cache misses, allocations, and work repeated every frame.

lessons.title: Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
lessons.summary: A program is not finished when it works on your machine. This lesson covers what it takes to put a tool or game in other people's hands and keep it working: reproducible Release builds, versioning with **semantic versions**, crash reports with symbols kept for every release, installers and updates, documentation, licences, and the habits of maintenance (changelogs, issue tracking, and deciding what not to build).

milestones.title: Capstone Projects
milestones.blurb: Larger projects that pull the whole course together.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
lessons.summary: The first capstone joins chapters 6, 12 and 14 into one polished tool: a read-only memory inspector for **programs you built yourself**, with a Dear ImGui interface showing the region map, a hex view with typed overlays, snapshots with change highlighting, and the telemetry channel from chapter 12. This lesson gives the specification, an architecture, the milestones in order, the acceptance tests and stretch goals.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
lessons.summary: The second capstone turns Delve into a game built to be modded, joining chapters 10, 11 and 13 with the security of chapter 17. Mods add data (levels, items, monsters), scripts and optional native plugins through a versioned API; a mod manager resolves load order and dependencies; the game survives broken mods. This lesson gives the specification, the mod format, the plugin API shape, milestones, acceptance tests and stretch goals.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
lessons.summary: The third capstone grows chapter 16's echo driver into **XenonLog**, a small, well-engineered driver and client pair that runs only in your lab virtual machine. The driver keeps a bounded in-kernel message log that clients append to and read back through versioned IOCTLs; the client is an ImGui tool with live statistics. The emphasis is engineering quality: validation, locking at the right IRQL, Driver Verifier, a fuzzing client, kernel debugging and a written design.

lessons.title: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
lessons.summary: The last capstone applies chapter 9's reverse engineering, chapter 8's debugging and chapter 7's assembly to a program whose source you have not read, and turns the findings into a clear technical report. Targets are chosen so the analysis is legal and checkable: open-source programs you build yourself with the source set aside, practice programs published for analysis, and programs a classmate writes for you. The lesson covers choosing a target, the method, the report's structure and how to check your conclusions against the truth.
